title: The basics
blurb: What Syneva is, what I refused to build into it, and why your verdict stays yours.

items.question: What is Syneva, in one sentence?
items.answer: An integrated review environment for code you didn’t write by hand: a local browser desk where you judge your agent’s diff, question it on the line, and hand a structured verdict back.

items.question: Does Syneva review code for me?
items.answer: No. You review the code. Your own agent can set the reading order and answer your questions. Syneva records your decisions and hands them back to that agent.

items.question: Does it ever auto-approve anything?
items.answer: Never. Every change starts pending, and only your keypress records a verdict. A verdict is stored on that exact change, not inferred from git staging.

items.question: What if the agent rewrites code I already accepted?
items.answer: Each change is content-hashed. On reload, a rewritten change resets to pending while untouched work keeps your verdict. Approvals and comment anchors follow the same rule.

items.question: What can I review?
items.answer: Your working tree, your staged changes, a branch or pull request against its merge-base, or a single file such as a plan. See Workflows.

title: Your agent
blurb: Bring the agent you already use. Here is what it may touch and what it gets back.

items.question: Which coding agents work with it?
items.answer: Any of them. The contract is plain JSON on stdout plus a localhost HTTP server. Syneva ships as a pi package, and Codex, Cursor or a shell script can drive the standalone CLI.

items.question: Do I need pi?
items.answer: No. pi gives you the smoothest loop (prompt templates, a correspondent thread for questions, a status command), but the CLI works on its own.

items.question: Does my agent edit files while I review?
items.answer: It shouldn’t, and the contract tells it so: answering a question is read-only, and edits happen between rounds, followed by syneva reload.

items.question: What exactly does my agent receive when I Send?
items.answer: A ReviewResult: what you accepted, rejected and requested, which files you approved or staged, any questions still open, and an optional overall note.

title: Your code and data
blurb: Your review stays on your machine. Here is where it lives and what survives a restart.

items.question: Where does my review live?
items.answer: On your machine, under ~/.syneva. Every save is persisted, and a hub restart restores every desk at the same URL, so your open tab heals itself.

items.question: Does Syneva send anything anywhere?
items.answer: No telemetry, no account, no model calls. The hub binds to loopback by default. Two honest footnotes: the desk loads its web fonts from Google Fonts, so your browser fetches them when a desk opens, and at most once a day, when a desk starts, the CLI asks the npm registry whether a newer version exists (set SYNEVA_NO_UPDATE_CHECK=1 to skip it).

items.question: Can I review from another machine?
items.answer: Yes, for remote-dev setups. Start the hub with --host and an access key (--key): you sign in once in the browser, your agents send the key. Without a key the hub refuses to bind beyond loopback unless you pass --insecure, which belongs only on a network you fully trust, like a personal tailnet.

items.question: What happens if I close the tab?
items.answer: Nothing is lost. The hub keeps the desk serving — it never closes a desk on its own — and a hub restart restores every desk with its review state at the same URL.

title: Limits and what’s next
blurb: What is still a prototype, what I am building next, and what it costs you.

items.question: Can I use the plan desk today?
items.answer: The dedicated plan desk is a prototype. You can already open a plan with syneva file plan.md and comment block by block.

items.question: What’s on the roadmap?
items.answer: In rough order: a command palette for every review action, commit, range and branch review modes, and lazy per-file loading with guards for very large and binary files.

items.question: Is it free?
items.answer: Yes. Syneva is open source under the MIT license.
